{{Short description|Generalized residue for several complex variables}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Poincaré residue''' is a generalization, to [[several complex variable]]s and [[complex manifold]] theory, of the [[residue at a pole]] of [[complex function theory]]. It is just one of a number of such possible extensions.

Given a hypersurface <math>X \subset \mathbb{P}^n</math> defined by a degree <math>d</math> polynomial <math>F</math> and a rational <math>n</math>-form <math>\omega</math> on <math>\mathbb{P}^n</math> with a pole of order <math>k > 0</math> on <math>X</math>, then we can construct a cohomology class <math>\operatorname{Res}(\omega) \in H^{n-1}(X;\mathbb{C})</math>. If <math>n=1</math> we recover the classical residue construction.

== Historical construction ==
When Poincaré first introduced residues<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Poincaré|first=H.|date=1887|title=Sur les résidus des intégrales doubles|url=https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.acta/1485888747|journal=Acta Mathematica|language=FR|volume=9|pages=321–380|doi=10.1007/BF02406742|issn=0001-5962|doi-access=free}}</ref> he was studying period integrals of the form<blockquote><math>\underset{\Gamma}\iint \omega</math> for <math>\Gamma \in H_2(\mathbb{P}^2 - D)</math></blockquote>where <math>\omega</math> was a rational differential form with poles along a divisor <math>D</math>. He was able to make the reduction of this integral to an integral of the form<blockquote><math>\int_\gamma \text{Res}(\omega)</math> for <math>\gamma \in H_1(D)</math></blockquote>where <math>\Gamma = T(\gamma)</math>, sending <math>\gamma</math> to the boundary of a solid <math>\varepsilon</math>-tube around <math>\gamma</math> on the smooth locus <math>D^*</math>of the divisor. If<blockquote><math>\omega = \frac{q(x,y)dx\wedge dy}{p(x,y)}</math></blockquote>on an affine chart where <math>p(x,y)</math> is irreducible of degree <math>N</math> and <math>\deg q(x,y) \leq N-3</math> (so there is no poles on the line at infinity<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Griffiths|first=Phillip A.|date=1982|title=Poincaré and algebraic geometry|url=https://www.ams.org/bull/1982-06-02/S0273-0979-1982-14967-9/|journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society|language=en|volume=6|issue=2|pages=147–159|doi=10.1090/S0273-0979-1982-14967-9|issn=0273-0979|doi-access=free}}</ref> <sup>page 150</sup>). Then, he gave a formula for computing this residue as<blockquote><math>\text{Res}(\omega) = -\frac{qdx}{\partial p / \partial y} = \frac{qdy}{\partial p / \partial x}</math></blockquote>which are both cohomologous forms.

== Construction ==

=== Preliminary definition ===
Given the setup in the introduction, let <math>A^p_k(X)</math> be the space of meromorphic <math>p</math>-forms on <math>\mathbb{P}^n</math> which have poles of order up to <math>k</math>. Notice that the standard differential <math>d</math> sends

:<math>d: A^{p-1}_{k-1}(X) \to A^p_k(X)</math>

Define

:<math>\mathcal{K}_k(X)  = \frac{A^p_k(X)}{dA^{p-1}_{k-1}(X)}</math>

as the '''rational de-Rham cohomology groups'''. They form a filtration<blockquote><math>\mathcal{K}_1(X) \subset \mathcal{K}_2(X) \subset \cdots \subset \mathcal{K}_n(X) =
H^{n+1}(\mathbb{P}^{n+1}-X)</math></blockquote>corresponding to the [[Jacobian ideal|Hodge filtration.]]

=== Definition of residue ===
Consider an <math>(n-1)</math>-cycle <math>\gamma \in H_{n-1}(X;\mathbb{C})</math>. We take a tube <math>T(\gamma)</math> around <math>\gamma</math> (which is locally isomorphic to <math>\gamma\times S^1</math>) that lies within the complement of <math>X</math>. Since this is an <math>n</math>-cycle, we can integrate a rational <math>n</math>-form <math>\omega</math> and get a number. If we write this as

:<math>\int_{T(-)}\omega : H_{n-1}(X;\mathbb{C}) \to \mathbb{C}</math>

then we get a linear transformation on the homology classes. Homology/cohomology duality implies that this is a cohomology class

:<math>\operatorname{Res}(\omega) \in H^{n-1}(X;\mathbb{C})</math>

which we call the residue. Notice if we restrict to the case <math>n=1</math>, this is just the standard residue from complex analysis (although we extend our meromorphic <math>1</math>-form to all of <math>\mathbb{P}^1</math>. This definition can be summarized as the map<blockquote><math>\text{Res}: H^{n}(\mathbb{P}^{n}\setminus X) \to H^{n-1}(X)</math></blockquote>

=== Algorithm for computing this class ===
There is a simple recursive method for computing the residues which reduces to the classical case of <math>n=1</math>. Recall that the residue of a <math>1</math>-form

:<math> \operatorname{Res}\left(\frac{dz} z  + a\right) = 1</math>

If we consider a chart containing <math>X</math> where it is the vanishing locus of <math>w</math>, we can write a meromorphic <math>n</math>-form with pole on <math>X</math> as

:<math>\frac{dw}{w^k}\wedge \rho</math>

Then we can write it out as

:<math> \frac{1}{(k-1)}\left( \frac{d\rho}{w^{k-1}} + d\left(\frac{\rho}{w^{k-1}}\right) \right)</math>

This shows that the two cohomology classes

:<math>\left[ \frac{dw}{w^k}\wedge \rho \right] = \left[ \frac{d\rho}{(k-1)w^{k-1}} \right]</math>

are equal. We have thus reduced the order of the pole hence we can use recursion to get a pole of order <math>1</math> and define the residue of <math>\omega</math> as

:<math> \operatorname{Res}\left( \alpha \wedge \frac{dw} w + \beta \right) = \alpha|_X</math>

== Example ==
For example, consider the curve <math>X \subset \mathbb{P}^2</math> defined by the polynomial

:<math>F_t(x,y,z) = t(x^3 + y^3 + z^3) - 3xyz</math>

Then, we can apply the previous algorithm to compute the residue of

:<math>\omega = \frac{\Omega}{F_t} = \frac{x\,dy\wedge dz - y \, dx\wedge dz + z \, dx\wedge dy}{t(x^3 + y^3 + z^3) - 3xyz}</math>

Since
:<math>
\begin{align}
-z\,dy\wedge\left( \frac{\partial F_t}{\partial x} \, dx + \frac{\partial F_t}{\partial y} \, dy + \frac{\partial F_t}{\partial z} \, dz \right) &=z\frac{\partial F_t}{\partial x} \, dx\wedge dy - z \frac{\partial F_t}{\partial z} \, dy\wedge dz \\
y \, dz\wedge\left(\frac{\partial F_t}{\partial x} \, dx + \frac{\partial F_t}{\partial y} \, dy + \frac{\partial F_t}{\partial z} \, dz\right) &= -y\frac{\partial F_t}{\partial x} \, dx\wedge dz - y \frac{\partial F_t}{\partial y} \, dy\wedge dz 
\end{align}
</math>
and
:<math>
3F_t - z\frac{\partial F_t}{\partial x} - y\frac{\partial F_t}{\partial y} = x \frac{\partial F_t}{\partial x}
</math>

we have that

:<math>
\omega = \frac{y\,dz - z\,dy}{\partial F_t / \partial x} \wedge \frac{dF_t}{F_t} + \frac{3\,dy\wedge dz}{\partial F_t/\partial x}
</math>

This implies that

:<math>\operatorname{Res}(\omega) = \frac{y\,dz - z\,dy}{\partial F_t / \partial x} </math>
